source_text: Καὶ ἰδοὺ Ἐλισάβετ ἡ συγγενής σου, καὶ αὐτὴ συνειληφυῖα υἱὸν ἐν γήρει αὐτῆς· καὶ οὗτος μὴν ἕκτος ἐστὶν αὐτῇ τῇ καλουμένῃ στείρα· ὅτι οὐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ πᾶν ῥῆμα. Εἰ τοίνυν μετὰ τὸν Γορπιαῖον μῆνα ἀρχὴν ἔλαβε συλλαμβάνειν ἡ Ἐλισάβετ, καθὼς ἀποδέδεικται, ἀριθμῆσαι ἐξ ἐκείνου δεῖ τοὺς μεταξὺ μῆνας ἕξ. Εἰσὶ τοίνυν οὗτοι οἱ μῆνες, Ὑπερβερεταῖος, Δῖος, Ἀπελλαῖος, Αὐδοναῖος, Περίτιος, Δύστρος. Μετὰ τοῦτον οὖν τὸν ἕκτον μῆνα ἀρχὴν ἡ Μαρία τῆς συλλήψεως ἔλαβεν· ὅθεν καὶ ἐννέα μῆνας ἀριθμοῦντες, εἰς τὸν παρόντα τοῦτον ἀπαντησόμεθα μῆνα. Ἔστιν οὖν ὁ πρῶτος μὴν τῆς συλλήψεως τοῦ Δεσπότου Ἀπρίλλιος, ὅς ἐστι Ξανθικός· μεθ' ὃν Ἀρτεμίσιος, Δέσιος, Πάνεμος, Λώϊος, Γορπιαῖος, Ὑπερβερεταῖος, Δῖος, Ἀπελλαῖος, καὶ οὗτος ὁ μὴν ὁ ἐνεστὼς, καθ' ὃν τὴν ἡμέραν ἐπιτελοῦμεν. Ἵνα δὲ καὶ σαφέστερον ὑμῖν πάλιν γένηται τὸ λεγόμενον, ἐν συντόμῳ τὰ αὐτὰ πάλιν ἀναλαβὼν, ἐρῶ πρὸς τὴν ὑμετέραν ἀγάπην· Ἅπαξ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ εἰσήρχετο μόνος ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς εἰς τὰ Ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων. Πότε δὲ τοῦτο ἐγίνετο; Ἐν τῷ μηνὶ τῷ Γορπιαίῳ. Τότε οὖν εἰσῆλθεν ὁ Ζαχαρίας εἰς τὰ Ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων· τότε καὶ εὐηγγελίσθη περὶ τοῦ Ἰωάννου. Ἀνεχώρησεν οὖν ἐκεῖθεν, καὶ ἤρξατο συλλαμβάνειν ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ. Μετὰ δὲ τὸν Γορπιαῖον, ἕκτον μῆνα ἐχούσης τῆς Ἐλισάβετ, ὅσπερ ἐστὶν ὁ Δύστρος, ἤρξατο συλλαμβάνειν λοιπὸν ἡ Μαρία. Ἀπὸ Ξανθικοῦ τοίνυν ἐννέα ἀριθμοῦντες μῆνας, εἰς τὸν παρόντα ἥξομεν μῆνα, καθ' ὃν ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ἐτέχθη. ʹ. Ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν περὶ τῆς ἡμέρας πάντα ὑμῖν δῆλα ἐποιήσαμεν· ἓν δὲ λοιπὸν εἰπὼν, καταπαύσω τὸν λόγον, τῷ κοινῷ διδασκάλῳ τῶν μειζόνων παραχωρήσας. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ πολλοὶ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἀκούοντες, ὅτι Θεὸς ἐτέχθη ἐν σαρκὶ, καταγελῶσι διασύροντες, καὶ πολλοὺς τῶν ἀφελεστέρων θορυβοῦσι καὶ ταράττουσιν· ἀναγκαῖον καὶ πρὸς ἐκείνους, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ταραττομένους εἰπεῖν, ὥστε μὴ θορυβεῖσθαί ποτε, ὑπὸ ἀφρόνων ἀνθρώπων ἀναπειθομένους, μήτε ταράττεσθαι ἐκ τοῦ τῶν ἀπίστων γέλωτος. Καὶ γὰρ τὰ παιδία τὰ μικρὰ πολλάκις γελᾷ, σπουδαιολογουμένων ἡμῶν καὶ περὶ τῶν ἀναγκαίων ἀσχολουμένων· ἀλλ' οὐ τῆς τῶν γελωμένων πραγμάτων εὐτελείας, ἀλλὰ τῆς τῶν γελώντων ἀνοίας τεκμήριον ὁ γέλως ἐστίν. Ὅπερ οὖν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἔστιν εἰπεῖν, ὅτι παίδων ἀνοητότερον σχεδὸν διακείμενοι, τὰ φρίκης ἄξια καὶ πολλοῦ θαύματος γέμοντα διασύρουσι, τὰ δὲ ἀληθῶς καταγέλαστα σεμνύνουσι καὶ περιστέλλουσιν. Ἀλλ' ὅμως καὶ τὰ ἡμέτερα παρ' ἐκείνοις γελώμενα ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκείας σεμνότητος μένει, οὐδὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ γέλωτος ἐκείνων εἰς τὴν ἑαυτῶν παραβλαπτόμενα δόξαν· καὶ τὰ αὐτῶν πανταχόθεν περιστελλόμενα τὴν οἰκείαν ἀσχημοσύνην ἐνδείκνυται. Π ῶς γὰρ οὐκ ἐσχάτης παραπληξίας, αὐτοὺς μὲν εὐολίσθους ὑπάρχοντας εἰς λίθους καὶ ξύλα καὶ εὐτελῆ ξόανα τοὺς ἑαυτῶν εἰσάγοντας θεοὺς, καὶ καθάπερ ἐν δεσμωτηρίῳ τινὶ ἀποκλείοντας, μηδὲν αἰσχρὸν ἡγεῖσθαι μήτε ποιεῖν, μήτε λέγειν· ἡμῖν δὲ ἐγκαλεῖν λέγουσιν, ὅτι ναὸν ἑαυτῷ κατασκευάσας ὁ Θεὸς ζῶντα ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου, δι' αὐτοῦ τὴν οἰκουμένην ὠφέλησε; Καὶ ποῖον ἔγκλημα τοῦτο; Εἰ γὰρ αἰσχρὸν, ἐν ἀνθρωπίνῳ σώματι Θεὸν οἰκῆσαι, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν λίθῳ καὶ ξύλῳ, καὶ τοσοῦτον, ὅσον λίθος καὶ ξύλον ἀτιμότερον ἀνθρώπου, εἰ μὴ ἄρα καὶ τῶν ἀναισθήτων τούτων ὑλῶν εὐτελέστερον τὸ γένος ἡμῶν αὐτοῖς εἶναι δοκεῖ.
thought_title: From Elizabeth's sixth month to the present month: the date of Christ's birth proved
orientation: Chrysostom is still proving the December date of Christ's birth by counting months from Zechariah's service in the Holy of Holies, and now turns to answer pagan mockery of the Incarnation.
pass_a_gloss: And behold Elizabeth your kinswoman, and she herself has conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren; because no word will be impossible with God. If therefore after the month Gorpiaios Elizabeth began to conceive, as has been shown, it is necessary to count from that point the six months in between. These therefore are the months: Hyperberetaios, Dios, Apellaios, Audonaios, Peritios, Dystros. After this sixth month therefore Mary received the beginning of the conception; from which point also counting nine months, we will arrive at this present month. The first month therefore of the conception of the Master is April, which is Xanthikos; after which Artemisios, Desios, Panemos, Loos, Gorpiaios, Hyperberetaios, Dios, Apellaios, and this present month, in which we celebrate the day. But in order that what is said may become clearer to you again, taking up the same things again in brief, I will speak to your love: Once in the year the high priest alone entered into the Holy of Holies. When did this happen? In the month Gorpiaios. At that time therefore Zechariah entered into the Holy of Holies; at that time also he received the good news about John. He departed therefore from there, and his wife began to conceive. After Gorpiaios, when Elizabeth had the sixth month, which is Dystros, Mary began to conceive from then on. Counting therefore nine months from Xanthikos, we will come to the present month, in which our Lord Jesus Christ was born. 2. But the things concerning the day we have made all clear to you; but saying one thing remaining, I will stop the discourse, yielding to the common teacher of the greater things. For since many of the Greeks, hearing that God was born in flesh, mock and disparage, and disturb and trouble many of the simpler ones; it is necessary to speak both to those and to those who are troubled, so that they may never be disturbed, being persuaded by foolish men, nor troubled by the laughter of the faithless. For also small children often laugh when we speak seriously and are occupied with necessary matters; but the laughter is not evidence of the worthlessness of the matters laughed at, but of the folly of those laughing. The very thing therefore it is possible to say also about the Greeks, that being disposed almost more foolishly than children, they disparage the things worthy of shuddering and full of much wonder, but honor and cover up the things truly laughable. But nevertheless also our things laughed at by them remain in their own dignity, being harmed in no way in their own glory by their laughter; and their things covered up from every side display their own shamefulness. For how is it not of extreme madness, that they themselves, being easily led astray into stones and wood and cheap idols, bringing in their own gods and shutting them up as in some prison, consider it shameful neither to do nor to say anything; but they accuse us, saying that God, having built for himself a living temple from the Holy Spirit, through it benefited the world? And what accusation is this? For if it is shameful for God to dwell in a human body, much more in stone and wood, and by so much as stone and wood is more dishonorable than a human being, unless indeed our race seems to them to be more worthless than these senseless materials.

choices.why: εὐόλισθος means 'slippery, easily slipping' in a moral sense of being prone to error or deception; the context is their being misled into idolatry, not physical slipping.

choices.term: ναὸν ἑαυτῷ κατασκευάσας ὁ Θεὸς ζῶντα ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου
choices.english: God, having built for himself a living temple from the Holy Spirit
choices.why: ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου modifies ζῶντα, indicating the temple's living quality originates from the Holy Spirit, not that the Spirit is the instrument by which God built it.

choices.term: τῷ κοινῷ διδασκάλῳ τῶν μειζόνων παραχωρήσας
choices.english: yielding to the common teacher of the greater things
choices.why: παραχωρήσας means yielding or giving place; Chrysostom defers to a shared teacher (likely Paul) for the greater matters, not simply 'handing over'.

choices.term: ἐν συντόμῳ τὰ αὐτὰ πάλιν ἀναλαβὼν
choices.english: taking up the same things again in brief
choices.why: ἀναλαβὼν means taking up or resuming; Chrysostom recapitulates the argument concisely for clarity.

choices.term: τὰ φρίκης ἄξια καὶ πολλοῦ θαύματος γέμοντα
choices.english: the things worthy of shuddering and full of much wonder
choices.why: φρίκη denotes shuddering awe or dread at the sacred; 'shuddering' preserves the reverential fear, not mere 'fear' or 'horror'.

choices.english: shutting them up as in some prison
choices.why: δεσμωτήριον is a prison; the image is of confining their gods in temples as if imprisoning them, which Chrysostom finds absurd.

pass_b_english: And behold, Elizabeth your relative has also conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren; for nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:36-37). If, then, Elizabeth began to conceive after the month of Gorpiaios, as has been shown, we must count six months from that point. Those months are Hyperberetaios, Dios, Apellaios, Audonaios, Peritios, and Dystros. After this sixth month, Mary began to conceive; and from there, counting nine months, we will arrive at the present month. The first month of the Lord’s conception, then, is April, which is Xanthikos; after it come Artemisios, Desios, Panemos, Loios, Gorpiaios, Hyperberetaios, Dios, Apellaios, and this present month, in which we celebrate the day. And so that what I am saying may become clearer to you again, let me take up the same things once more in brief and speak to your love. Once a year the high priest alone entered the Holy of Holies. When did this happen? In the month of Gorpiaios. At that time, then, Zechariah entered the Holy of Holies; at that time he also received the good news about John. He departed from there, and his wife began to conceive. After Gorpiaios, when Elizabeth was in her sixth month—which is Dystros—Mary then began to conceive. Counting nine months from Xanthikos, then, we will come to the present month, in which our Lord Jesus Christ was born.

But we have made everything about the day clear to you. One thing remains for me to say, and then I will bring my discourse to a close, yielding to the common teacher of the greater things. For since many of the Greeks, when they hear that God was born in flesh, mock and disparage it, and they disturb and trouble many of the simpler ones, it is necessary to speak both to them and to those who are troubled, so that they may never be disturbed, persuaded by foolish people, nor troubled by the laughter of the unbelieving. For small children often laugh when we speak seriously and are occupied with necessary matters; but the laughter is evidence not of the worthlessness of the things being laughed at, but of the folly of those who laugh. The same can be said of the Greeks: they are disposed almost more foolishly than children, disparaging the things worthy of shuddering and full of much wonder, while they honor and protect the things that are truly laughable. But nevertheless, the things of ours that are laughed at by them remain in their own dignity, suffering no harm to their own glory from that laughter; and the things of theirs that are protected from every side display their own shamefulness. For how is it not the height of madness that they, being easily led astray into stones and wood and cheap carved images, bring in their own gods and shut them up as in some prison, and consider it no shame either to do or to say anything—yet they accuse us, saying that God, having built for himself a living temple from the Holy Spirit, through it benefited the world? What kind of accusation is this? For if it is shameful for God to dwell in a human body, it is far more shameful for him to dwell in stone and wood—and so much more, as stone and wood are more dishonorable than a human being, unless indeed our race seems to them to be of less value than these senseless materials.

last_rejected.source_quote: αὐτοὺς μὲν εὐολίσθους ὑπάρχοντας εἰς λίθους καὶ ξύλα
last_rejected.why: 'εὐολίσθους' means 'prone to slip/fall' (morally susceptible), not 'easily led astray into'; the Greek says they themselves slip into worshipping stones and wood.
last_rejected.fix: they themselves being prone to slip into stones and wood
last_rejected.ruling: εὐολίσθους means prone to slipping; 'easily led astray' is a legitimate figurative rendering within normal range.

last_rejected.why: Agency confused: subject is 'they' (the Greeks), but 'εἰσάγοντας' and 'ἀποκλείοντας' are accusative participles describing their gods, not what the Greeks do to them. The gods are brought in and shut up.
last_rejected.fix: bringing in gods and shutting them up as in some prison
last_rejected.ruling: εἰσάγοντας and ἀποκλείοντας are accusative participles governed by αὐτοὺς; the Greeks bring in and shut up their gods. Translation is correct.

last_rejected.why: The infinitives 'ποιεῖν' and 'λέγειν' depend on 'ἡγεῖσθαι': 'considering nothing shameful neither to do nor to say'—the Greeks consider nothing shameful, not that they do/say anything without shame.
last_rejected.fix: considering nothing shameful, neither to do nor to say
last_rejected.ruling: μηδὲν αἰσχρὸν ἡγεῖσθαι μήτε ποιεῖν μήτε λέγειν: 'consider nothing shameful to do or say' is accurately rendered; no meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: God, having built for himself a living temple from the Holy Spirit
last_rejected.source_quote: ὅτι ναὸν ἑαυτῷ κατασκευάσας ὁ Θεὸς ζῶντα ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου
last_rejected.why: 'ἑαυτῷ' is dative 'for himself', but 'ζῶντα' is accusative agreeing with 'ναὸν' (living temple), not 'from the Holy Spirit' as agent; 'ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου' means 'by/from the Holy Spirit' as source, but 'living' modifies 'temple'.
last_rejected.fix: God having prepared for himself a living temple by the Holy Spirit
last_rejected.ruling: ζῶντα modifies ναὸν (living temple) and ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου is source; English 'living temple from the Holy Spirit' captures both correctly.
